ItaLean 2025: Bridging Formal Mathematics and AI

We are pleased to announce ItaLean 2025, an international conference dedicated to advancing the formalisation of mathematics in Lean and exploring the interplay between formal methods and machine learning.

Dates

9 – 12 December 2025.

Location

University of Bologna, jointly hosted by the Departments of Mathematics, Physics and Astronomy, and Computer Science.

Abstract

ItaLean 2025 brings together researchers and practitioners working at the intersection of Formal Mathematics and AI4Maths. The program will feature:

  • Invited lectures
  • Hands-on tutorials
  • Research talks from academia and industry
  • Product demonstrations
  • Panel discussion

We expect to welcome around 150 participants, including invited speakers, guests, and attendees selected through an application process.

Applications

Applications to participate in ItaLean 2025 are now open.

  • Priority deadline: 31 October 2025.
  • Cost: Participation is free of charge and includes access to all conference sessions.
  • Financial support: A limited amount of accommodation support may be available; applicants can indicate their need for support in the application form.
  • Supporting material: Applicants are encouraged to include a CV with their submission.

Apply here!

Program

A preliminary schedule will be released in the coming weeks, with regular updates thereafter.

Organisers

@Eugenio Cainelli (University of Bologna)
@Lorenzo Luccioli (University of Bologna)
@Marco Lenci (University of Bologna)
@Pietro Monticone (University of Trento)
@Giovanni Paolini (University of Bologna)
@Claudio Sacerdoti Coen (University of Bologna)

Further information

For more details, updates, and announcements, please visit the official website:
https://pitmonticone.github.io/ItaLean2025/.

We warmly encourage researchers, students, and practitioners interested in Lean, formal mathematics, and AI to apply and join us in Bologna this December.

We look forward to seeing many of you at ItaLean 2025!
The conference has now been added to the “Upcoming events” section of the Lean Community website https://leanprover-community.github.io/events.html.

The preliminary schedule for ItaLean 2025 is now online: https://pitmonticone.github.io/ItaLean2025.

It includes the current draft of the talk programme, tutorials, project-work sessions, and all planned events. Minor adjustments may still happen as we finalise speaker availability and logistics, but the overall structure is already stable.

Hi everyone!

The maintainers of the Sphere Packing Project are thrilled to announce a Sphere Packing Autoformalisation Challenge in partnership with the organisers of the ItaLean conference taking place in Bologna from 9-12 December, 2025.

We have been in contact with a number of AI companies who have expressed an interest in contributing to our project. In fact, we have already merged PRs to our repository that were co-authored by Aristotle and Gauss. Given that a number of AI companies will be at ItaLean, we thought it would be the perfect platform to showcase just how far the AI for Mathematics industry has come!

What's in it for you?

There are numerous benefits to taking part in our challenge. Chief amongst them are the following:

  1. You get a chance to demonstrate to the world that your agents are good enough to contribute to the formalisation of a Fields Medal-winning result.
  2. You will receive detailed feedback and comments on your model's performance from people familiar with both the mathematics of the proof and the technicalities of its formalisation.

Timeline and logistics:

Here’s how the challenge will work.

  1. To gather information about how the model interaction looks from a user's perspective, we request that those who want to take part in the challenge give us a way of calling their models directly. Please share setup instructions with us by 2025-12-02T12:00:00-05:00. In the meantime, you are free to train your models on our repository and on whatever version of Mathlib you think is most appropriate.
  2. By 2025-12-02T12:00:00-05:00, we will put together a LaTeX document with a few challenge problems from our project. Our document will be designed with autoformalisation agents in mind: we will break complex proofs into simpler, more modular lemmas, and we will provide either informal proofs or code references for any dependencies of the theorems in our document. The dependencies may have sorrys in them, but we will not expect your models to prove them.
  3. We will create a private fork of the Sphere Packing Repository where we will run your autoformalisation agents on our LaTeX document at a randomly chosen time between 2025-12-02T12:00:00-05:00 and 2025-12-07T12:00:00-05:00.
  4. We will run each model only once on each problem in our document, and we will disregard any submissions that a model takes over 24 hours to come up with.
  5. At ItaLean, we will make the fork public and release our PDF with the challenge problems. We will, at that point, invite all members of the community to review the autoformalisations and initiate the process of merging code from the fork into the main repository.

The Spirit of this Challenge

Something we cannot emphasise enough is that this is a challenge, not a competition. The idea really is to showcase the power of all the models that participate. In the end, I anticipate that we will merge at least one lemma written by each model that participates. Note that we will have multiple challenge problems from various parts of the project that come from different areas of mathematics: while we will run each model on all the problems, it would be possible for two models to have zero overlap in what they manage to autoformalise!

The true spirit of this challenge is collaboration, whether it's human-human, human-machine, or even machine-machine. We really want this challenge to catalyse the collaboration we are already seeing between AI companies and mathematicians. If nothing else, we hope it leads to many a stimulating conversation in Bologna.

Interested in participating?

Get in touch with @Chris Birkbeck (Sphere Packing maintainer), @Seewoo Lee (Sphere Packing maintainer), @Lorenzo Luccioli (ItaLean organiser), @Pietro Monticone (ItaLean organiser), @David Renshaw (Institute for Computer-Aided Reasoning in Mathematics) or myself (Sphere Packing maintainer)! You can also drop in on our Packathons on 2025-11-24T11:00:00-05:00 and 2025-12-01T11:00:00-05:00 and talk to us there. We look forward to working with you!

Acknowledgements

The Sphere Packing project maintainers would like to extend our sincerest appreciation to the organisers of ItaLean and the NSF-funded Institute for Computer-Aided Reasoning in Mathematics based at Carnegie Mellon University. It would not have been possible to organise a challenge like this without your support!

Hi all! In light of Thanksgiving, we have decided to push the participation deadline to 2 December 12 noon Eastern Time. This will also give any interested parties a second opportunity to talk to us at a Packathon. I have updated my previous message to reflect this. Happy Thanksgiving!

Hi everyone!

We were very happy to see that our challenge attracted a great deal of interest, both from prospective participants and the broader community. Unfortunately, of everybody interested in taking part, the majority found our timeline to be too tight. We have therefore decided to postpone the challenge by a few months in order to maximise participation.

We are grateful to the ItaLean organisers for their support - it is indeed unfortunate that we cannot combine this challenge with what promises to be a wonderful conference. When the time is right, we will run the challenge under the aegis of the Institute for Computer-Aided Reasoning in Mathematics. In the meantime, we will continue to welcome AI contributions to our project and engage with both prospective participants and the broader community to ensure our challenge effectively achieves its objective of showcasing the power of autoformalisation technology.

Aristotle was ready :muscle::grinning:. While we are bummed that challenge is off, we’d still love to engage with the community on our results from SpherePacking. 

Here are some results from running on the repo with human intervention only for golfing/cleanup. The original unmodified Aristotle outputs are linked in the PRs as well.

Some examples of Aristotle both proving results, and finding issues with stated theorems:

  • Aristotle completed the proof of the calculation step in the Cohn-Elkies linear programming bound (spherepacking#211)
  • Aristotle proved that the principal congruence subgroup Γ(2) is generated by the matrices α, β and -I (spherepacking#217).
  • Aristotle proved the exponential decay bound for the quasimodular form φ₀ (spherepacking#222).
  • Aristotle found counterexamples (spherepacking#218, spherepacking#215) and automatically fixed a misformalized statement by adding a missing hypothesis (spherepacking#218).

We continue to be excited about getting your feedback, and would love to hear what you think at #mathlib4 > Discussion thread for Aristotle API. All of these results, and the ones you might find on twitter, are obtained from external users using the public API. As always, anyone can sign up for access here – it’s free!
